author: Forbes
description:
At the Forbes 30/50 Summit, moderator Maggie McGrath, Forbes Women editor, hosts a compelling panel featuring Francine Katsoudas, EVP and Chief People, Policy & Purpose Officer at Cisco, and Dr. Maryam Bin Mashar, Human-AI Interaction Researcher, USC Marshall School of Business. 

Together, they explore the real-world impact of artificial intelligence on careers, psychological relationships, workplace skills, and personal purpose. From overcoming the gender gap in AI usage to handling AI feedback, preserving authentic human connections, and retraining entry-level talent, this discussion offers actionable strategies for leading in an AI-driven world without losing human judgment.

author: Forbes
description:
Inside BMW’s Exclusive Performance Center Delivery Program

For luxury automobile buyers, picking up a custom-ordered vehicle can extend far beyond the showroom floor. Through BMW Performance Center Delivery (PCD), customers ordering a new vehicle can bypass traditional dealership handoffs to receive their car directly at BMW’s facility in Greer, South Carolina—located adjacent to its primary U.S. manufacturing hub.

Because the program is restricted to approximately 1,400 deliveries annually due to facility capacity limits, Performance Center Director Dan Gubitosa emphasizes that the operation is designed as a deep brand immersion platform. Beyond driving similar models on the proving grounds track, new owners undergo an intensive, tailored orientation with a dedicated Product Specialist.

author: Forbes
description:
NBA teams don’t come up for sale often—two-thirds of the league’s control owners have been in place for at least a decade—which is one big reason why it was such a surprise that August featured two quick flips. First, Mark Walter agreed to sell the Los Angeles Lakers to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger only about ten months after his purchase of the franchise had closed, and then, barely a week later, Minnesota Timberwolves limited partner Marc Stad reached an agreement to buy out Marc Lore, 14 months after the retail billionaire had officially taken over.

Both deals still await approval by the NBA’s board of governors, but assuming they close without incident, as expected, it will mean a tidy return for the sellers. Lore, who first agreed to buy the Timberwolves and the WNBA’s Minnesota Lynx in 2021 in a multi-stage transaction with an enterprise value of $1.5 billion, got $4.5 billion for the two clubs—a 25% annual return even when measured from the initial agreement.
